name: Indiana

notes: Food for home consumption is exempt; candy, soft drinks and dietary supplements are taxed at 7%, which is not counted here.

Cigarettes and other tobacco are taxed at 7%, on top of excise taxes left out here: $2.995 a pack of cigarettes, 30% of the wholesale price on other tobacco and closed-system vapor cartridges, and 30% of the retail price on e-liquid and open-system vapor products (all since July 1, 2025).
Household supplies: children's diapers have been exempt since August 5, 2022, as reported (not confirmed with the Department of Revenue), which is not taken out here.
Personal care products: menstrual products are taxed at 7%; a House budget proposal to exempt them and adult diapers was reported, but no enactment was found.
Barber and beauty services aren't taxed.
Laundry and dry cleaning services aren't taxed.

Gasoline carries a 7% gasoline use tax in place of sales tax (26.5 cents a gallon for November 2026) plus a 37-cent excise tax, left out here; the governor's energy emergency order suspended collection of both through November 4, 2026, so the 7% counted here resumes November 5.
Repair labor is not taxed when it is separately stated (2017 FTA survey answer; not re-verified with the Department of Revenue).
Hotel stays pay county innkeeper's taxes (Marion County 10%), which are not counted here.
gaps: No local general sales taxes in Indiana. Food and beverage taxes on restaurant meals are counted in the restaurant rate: 15 counties (Marion 2%, the others 1%) and 29 cities and towns (their own rate plus their county's, as the Department of Revenue adds them). Greendale's tax starts after the date used and is noted on its page; Centerville's, adopted but not on the Department's list, is noted on its page.

programs: Tax increment financing districts are mapped for Indianapolis and Marion County, Bloomington, Muncie and Delaware County, South Bend, Goshen, and Evansville and Vanderburgh County, from each city's or county's own layer. The state's layer of counties' TIF boundaries (Indiana Geographic Information Office, 44 counties) has no status and includes residential TIF areas, and Hamilton County's (266 allocation areas and amendments) has no status either, so neither is shown; Fort Wayne's, Allen County's and Lake County's TIFs have no other map. Indianapolis's two economic improvement districts are mapped; Downtown Indy's Economic Enhancement District (2024) isn't drawn. Urban enterprise zones (IEDC) and Main Street communities have no statewide map.

warn.text: Indianapolis draws many visitors, most of all downtown (conventions, sports and the Indianapolis 500), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (0.2%) and its 316 lodging places (0.4 per 1,000 residents) are spread over a large city. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local, most of all downtown.

Michigan City draws many summer visitors (the lakefront, Indiana Dunes and its outlet mall), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (4.4%) and its 30 lodging places (1.0 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Porter County draws many visitors to Indiana Dunes National Park, but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (1.2%) and lodging places (0.3 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.

Spencer County draws many visitors to Santa Claus (Holiday World), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (2.0%) and lodging places (0.6 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
